subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for a Genshin-style red panda balancing on a mossy stone, with a creature skeleton (spine, neck, head, jaw, legs, ringed tail, ears) and a stone base featuring moss and small glowing flowers.

I'm scaling the panda to roughly 0.6m body and 0.45m tail, posed standing on a ~0.5m boulder with legs spread and tail lifted for balance, totaling about 0.7m in height, and sketching the boulder's low-poly lathe outline as a separate prop from the jointed creature geometry.

For rigging, I need the stone to stay static rather than move with the panda's animated bones, so I'm adding a dedicated "root" joint near the ground to anchor it, with "hips" as a child joint, rather than binding the stone directly to a leg or hip joint.

Now I'm working out the panda's pose dimensions: standing on the stone top at y≈0.31, body center around y=0.51 with short legs, facing +Z with hips and shoulders offset along z. I need to widen the stone's top radius to about 0.3 so the panda's feet (spread roughly 0.14 apart in x and 0.3 in z) fit comfortably on top, though the lathe tool doesn't support non-uniform scaling directly.

I'm narrowing the stance for a more balanced look -- shorter body with hips/shoulders closer together and feet gathered near the center, verifying the foot-to-stone-center distance stays within the top plateau radius of 0.24-0.26. I'm sizing the stone with a base radius of 0.36 tapering to 0.26 at top, and considering a raised tail curving upward over the stone's edge to sell the "balancing" pose while keeping all four paws planted.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: setting the hip joint around y=0.49 with the body's belly clearance at roughly 0.09 above the stone top for a fluffy silhouette, then building a spine chain from hips to chest using a curved path with three joints parented under the hips.

Setting up the chain with 3 spans named hips, spine, and chest, parented at root with the spine role.

Then I'm adding a short neck chain from the chest tip up to the head base, using 3 points for 2 spans named neck1 and neck2, parented to the chest joint.

Next I'm placing a head joint at the top of the neck, aimed slightly forward and down, and starting to build the skull geometry as a scaled sphere positioned relative to the head's local frame for a red panda's broad, short-snouted face.

I'm sketching the facial features: wide cheeks via scaled sphere dimensions, iconic white cheek tufts made from small cones angled outward, and a short cream-colored muzzle positioned forward and slightly below the skull.

Continuing with a small dark rounded nose at the snout tip, a separate hinged jaw piece made from a scaled cream sphere, and planning big triangular ears with white inner fur using extruded leaf shapes positioned up and outward on the head.

Working out ear orientation vectors...

Defining ear geometry...

I'm working out the orthogonal basis vectors for the ear tilt using a rotation angle, confirming the geometry stays symmetric. Now I'm settling on the red panda's Genshin-style cel-shaded coloring—rusty orange coat, cream accents, dark brown limbs—and planning the amber-eyed decal placement on the skull mesh.

I'm positioning the eye decals via azimuthal coordinates around the skull center, then designing the facial markings: white eyebrow spots and dark red tear-mark stripes using position-based fur edge paints, with a cream threshold cut around the lower face based on the head's y-coordinate range.

For the body, I'm defining underside shading with a fur edge paint transitioning from orange on top to dark brown on the belly, then working out loft stations along a spine chain from rump to chest, making sure station positions extend slightly beyond the chain's endpoints to properly shape the body volume.

Now I'm setting up the tail as a separate chain parented to the hip joint, confirming that loft sections skin correctly along the bone chain, and positioning the four legs so the paws rest naturally on top of the stone surface—adjusting paw height relative to the stone's top plane so the feet sit just above it without clipping through.

For the limbs, I'm working out segment lengths and bend directions so each leg naturally bends between joint and target: front legs get a two-segment chain (shoulder, elbow, paw) with elbow bending backward, while hind legs need a three-segment chain (hip, knee, hock, foot) with alternating forward/backward bends so the foot lands flat and the proportions stay anatomically plausible for a red panda.

Deciding this is getting fragile with too many variables, I'm simplifying to robust two-bone legs for both front and hind, computing hip-to-target distances to pick lengths like 0.08 each with the knee bending forward, and planning tube geometry with tapering radius from thigh to paw, plus small sphere/cone toe details in dark brown to finish the paw look.

I'm also sketching the tail now—thick, ringed, curving up and back from the base in an S-shape for a balanced pose, matching the dark leg color with maybe a lighter tip.

Wait, I need to check whether cel's shading function actually passes the segment parameter s to the paint—looking at the resolve signature, it seems shading calls resolve(base,p,n) without s, so any paint relying on s inside cel might not get that data.

Instead I'll use bands for the tail: a sweep with multiple color stops where each stop is itself a cel paint, alternating a lighter orange and a darker ring color, ending with a dark brownish tip. Since sweep splits the mesh at shared vertices per band, this should give a clean ringed tail with the end cap picking up the final band's dark tip color.

For fur, I'm considering a few small cone tufts along the tail for fluffiness but will keep it minimal to avoid complexity, then move on to head details like cheek tufts.

For cheek tufts, I'm placing small cream spikes on each side of the head pointing outward and back, attaching them to the head bone with explicit local coordinates for position and direction.

Confirming that "left" in local-space maps to positive X, matching the joint naming convention where s=1 is the left side. Now I'm working out eye placement — using decals sized around 0.042 by 0.058, positioned on the skull's face with azimuth near ±32° and slight elevation, anchored to the skull part.

I'm checking that the eyes won't be obscured by the muzzle: the skull's front surface sits around z=0.145, while the muzzle protrudes further to about z=0.165. At the eyes' azimuth their x-position lands around 0.05, close enough to the muzzle's half-width of 0.04 that there's some risk of overlap near the back of the muzzle, so I'm tracing through the geometry to confirm they stay clear.

Since this is a chibi-style design, I'll enlarge the skull scale to make the head proportionally bigger relative to the body, shrink the muzzle slightly, and widen the eye placement to around ±40° azimuth to avoid any overlap. I'm also planning to add simple SVG decal tear markings running from under the eyes down toward the mouth, using the mirror property so the left eye mirrors correctly per the documented convention.

I'm adding small cream eyebrow dots above the eyes using tiny sphere geometry, then shifting to face shading — using position-based fur coloring to make the lower face and cheeks cream while keeping the upper face red, which matches the classic red panda coloring pattern. I'm also considering a slight upward head tilt and how that affects the eye and cheek positioning.

For the finer details I'm planning dark cel-shaded ears with cream interiors, a small dark nose sphere at the muzzle tip, and skipping whiskers and a defined mouth line for simplicity. I'm also planning to break up the stone's perfect lathe silhouette with small boulder details, flattened moss clumps draping the top edges, and maybe a cluster of small glowing flowers or a luminous mushroom near the base for a touch of magical flair.

Now I'm considering adding glowing cyan-green mushrooms at the stone's base — cream stem cylinders topped with a glowing hemisphere cap — plus a small bamboo clump nearby with segmented stalks, node rings, and leaf shapes extruded along a plane, keeping the whole arrangement within a modest height budget.

I'm thinking of adding a handful of tiny glowing dendro motes floating nearby as extra sparkle, roughly five or six small octahedra with a soft yellow-green glow scattered around the base—decorative without interfering with the model's footprint.
